title: Characteristics of runners, recorded sessions and the participation panel
note: Percentages use the denominator for the corresponding group. SD denotes standard deviation. Q1 and Q3 denote the 25th and 75th percentiles. Blank cells indicate that the statistic is inapplicable or was not reported. ᵃFitRec records gender as reported by the provider. Categories with fewer than 10 runners are pooled. Neither source file records age. ᵇThe heart rate summary covers 106,341 sessions from at least 810 runners with at least one reading of 40 to 220 beats·min⁻¹. The sensitivity analyses use eligible sessions in their respective samples. Lower bounds protect counts that could disclose groups of fewer than 10 runners by subtraction. ᶜCalendar years are grouped so that each category includes at least 10 runners. ᵈCountry was assigned from the representative session location. Of the 28 countries with at least 100 sessions and 10 runners, the four with the most sessions are shown separately. ᵉThe daily maximum is the highest hourly ERA5-Land air temperature on the local calendar day in the grid cell for the session. The count at or above 25 °C includes sessions at or above 30 °C. ᶠHeat avoided is session temperature minus the daily maximum. A negative value indicates that the session took place in cooler conditions than the day’s hottest hour. ᵍThe participation denominator is the number of runner-days with a daily maximum at the runner’s most frequently used weather grid cell.

title: Within-runner changes in training, heart rate and participation at high daily maximum temperatures
note: Both contrasts use the median daily maximum (P50, 15.40 °C) as the reference. The main models used 106,600 sessions from 820 runners and included runner fixed effects, a three-knot restricted cubic spline for daily maximum temperature, seasonal terms and day-of-week indicators. Table S3 gives the pre-specified estimates with additional calendar-year indicators. Confidence intervals (CI) are pointwise and p values are two-sided, with standard errors clustered by runner. Heat avoided is session temperature minus the daily maximum. The within-day temperature rank compares session temperature with that day’s hourly temperatures. ᵃHolm adjustment applies to the four primary outcomes at P95. All other p values are nominal. Percentage changes for log-transformed outcomes equal 100[exp(contrast)-1]. Linear probability models give changes in percentage points. Changes in fractional rank are multiplied by 100 to give percentile points. ᵇHeart rate estimates use 106,341 sessions from at least 810 runners with a reading between 40 and 220 beats·min⁻¹. ᶜSteady-speed estimates use 18,626 sessions from at least 660 runners with eligible segments. ᵈParticipation estimates use 503,410 runner-days from 729 runners. Runner-by-year-month effects absorb the seasonal and calendar terms, so the main and pre-specified participation estimates coincide.

title: Selection of sessions and runners
note: ᵃRunner counts are exact unless shown as a lower bound under the disclosure rule. We report a lower bound when an exact count would differ from another published total by 1 to 9 runners. Sessions lack a daily maximum when any hour of the local day is missing from the downloaded weather windows, mainly on the first or last day of a window.

title: P95 versus P50 contrasts across four nested models
note: ᵃColumn (1) contains the exposure spline only; (2) adds the pre-specified controls (two annual sine–cosine pairs and day-of-week indicators, or, for the fixed-speed model, the seasonal pairs, the segment-speed spline, recorded running time over 14 days and the 28-day fitness proxy); (3) adds runner fixed effects and is the main specification; (4) adds calendar-year indicators and is the pre-specified specification. The exposure is the daily maximum (P50 15.40, P95 30.51 °C), except for fixed-speed heart rate, which uses session temperature (P50 12.61, P95 25.93 °C). Intervals are pointwise 95% confidence intervals from runner-clustered standard errors. The sequence was estimated on the samples of the main analyses (106,600 sessions; heart-rate models ≥106,340 sessions; fixed-speed model 19,350 sessions).

title: Main and pre-specified models and contrasts for the planned temperature comparisons
note: ᵃPanel A compares the main specification (runner fixed effects, daily-maximum spline, two annual sine–cosine pairs and day-of-week indicators, or, for the fixed-speed model, the session-temperature and speed splines, two training-history terms and the seasonal pairs) with the pre-specified specification, which also included calendar-year indicators. The main specification is the third of four nested specifications, which added controls, runner effects and calendar-year indicators in turn. ᵇPanel B reports the contrasts named in the analysis plan, at 25 and 30 °C relative to 20 °C, under the pre-specified specification; Holm's adjustment applies to the four primary outcomes at 30 °C, as planned. These estimates use the corrected heart-rate outcome (mean of readings from 40 to 220 beats per minute); before that correction the 30 °C heart-rate contrast was -0.11 (-0.81, 0.60). Percentage changes are 100[exp(contrast)-1]; probabilities and fractional ranks are multiplied by 100. The weekend rows are the planned effect modification, the weekend minus the weekday contrast; the planned joint tests of the two weekend-by-spline interaction terms gave p < 0.001 for heat avoided, p = 0.957 for speed, p = 0.656 for duration and p = 0.001 for heart rate. ᶜPanel C is the decomposition named in the analysis plan, at a daily maximum of 30 °C relative to 20 °C under the pre-specified specification. The original benchmark holds the reference-day gap between session temperature and the daily maximum constant, and the offset shares are fractions of that benchmark. Intervals use the normal delta method with the component fits treated as independent.

title: Sensitivity of heart-rate estimates to model specification, season, location and recording
note: ᵃIn panel A, fixed-speed models use the 19,350-session cohort and session-temperature percentiles (P50 12.61, P90 23.22, P95 25.93 °C) unless stated; common sessions are the 18,626 sessions of the main sample that also met the steady-speed criteria, where models of the daily maximum use its main-cohort percentiles. All rows in panel A are in beats·min⁻¹. The steady-segment models keep the controls of the fixed-speed model (seasonal pairs, recorded running time in the previous 14 days and 28-day median speed), with or without the segment-speed spline; the whole-session row with the same controls changes only the outcome. In panel B, runner-by-year-month effects compare each runner's days within the same calendar month and absorb the seasonal terms; runner-by-cell effects compare sessions of the same runner in the same 10-km weather cell; the usual-cell sample keeps the 68.6% of sessions recorded at each runner's most frequent cell (≥73,080 sessions, ≥810 runners). In panel C, participation rows use the 503,410 runner-days of 729 runners with runner-by-year-month effects and day-of-week indicators. Any recorded run uses every recorded running workout in the source metadata, including those without heart rate, dated in the runner's usual time zone. The heart-rate recording rows use ≥197,630 recorded runs in the participation windows, of which 55.0% carried heart rate, with the daily maximum at the usual cell. Panel D gives paired differences between the steady-segment and whole-session models of panel A in the same 18,626 sessions, with the joint runner-clustered covariance of the stacked fits; for the speed-free pair this equals the regression of the session-level difference on the same terms. In panel E, the time-weighted mean integrates heart rate over intervals of 30 s or less after removing isolated spikes (changes of more than 3 beats per minute per second into and out of a reading) and flat lines (identical readings for 120 s or more); common sessions are those with a time-weighted mean (≥18,610). Table S9 shows the share of the expected heart-rate rise that remained unexplained under each specification. These checks were specified after the pre-specified results were available and fixed before estimation (panels A to C on 4 November 2026 and panels D and E in the plan described in Section B.2.1). Intervals are pointwise 95% confidence intervals from runner-clustered standard errors.

title: Sampling interval, device recording limit and heart-rate contrasts
note: The main specification has runner fixed effects, two annual sine–cosine pairs aligned by hemisphere and day-of-week indicators. Intervals are pointwise 95% runner-clustered CR1 intervals with t critical values. The heart-rate models of panels B and C have no day-of-week indicators, as in the main fixed-speed model. Records hold at most 500 readings spread over the session; the median interval between readings comes from the raw time stamps of each session. Groups are terciles of that interval in the fixed-speed cohort (ties at whole seconds make them unequal) and capped against uncapped records. ᵃEach model interacts the exposure spline with the group indicators; the interaction p is the joint Wald test of those terms. Specified before estimation (Section B.2.2).

title: P90 and P95 contrasts relative to P50 with and without adjustment for sunrise and sunset
note: The main specification has runner fixed effects, two annual sine–cosine pairs aligned by hemisphere and day-of-week indicators. Intervals are pointwise 95% runner-clustered CR1 intervals with t critical values. ᵃSunrise and sunset are local clock times (hours) on the date of the session at its mean GPS position, from the NOAA solar-position equations (solar zenith 90.833°) and the IANA zone of the session with its historical rules, entered as two linear terms. Panel A uses the ≥106,540 sessions with a sunrise and a sunset (polar days excluded); each row compares the two fits on the same sessions, and the difference uses their joint runner-clustered covariance. Duration is shown as the percentage change, 100 × (exp(R) − 1), and its difference in log points × 100. Panel B computes sunrise and sunset at the centre of each runner's usual cell with the usual zone. Specified before estimation (Section B.3.1).

title: Run start times in relation to daylight and seasonal clock changes
note: The main specification has runner fixed effects, two annual sine–cosine pairs aligned by hemisphere and day-of-week indicators. ᵃIntervals are pointwise 95% runner-clustered CR1 intervals with t critical values. In panel A, 7.2% of sessions started before sunrise and 17.0% at or after sunset; probabilities are in percentage points. Panel B uses ≥23,080 sessions from ≥660 runners in 76 time zones that changed clocks, within 21 local days either side of a change (the change date counts as after). The model has an indicator for days after the change for each direction, separate linear slopes in days before and after each change, day-of-week indicators, the daily-maximum spline and fixed effects for each runner and change. The share is (forward jump − backward jump)/120. For the local clock start time it is near 1 if start times follow the sun and near 0 if they follow the clock; for start minus sunrise the same share is the clock-time share minus 1, so near 0 if start times follow the sun and near −1 if they follow the clock. Specified before estimation (Section B.3.1).

title: Decomposition of the expected heart-rate response, fixed-hour comparison and joint tests
note: Daily-maximum contrasts use P95 (30.51 °C) or P90 (27.64 °C) versus P50 (15.40 °C) of the main cohort. The decomposition applies the fixed-speed temperature response to the session temperatures implied by these maxima and by modelled heat avoided; the speed term applies the steady-speed response around the typical segment speed (3.190 m·s⁻¹) to the change in whole-session median speed. These quantities assume additivity and do not represent causal mediation; shares are fractions. Intervals use the normal delta method, with the joint runner-clustered covariance of the two heat-avoided fits and independent blocks otherwise, and therefore differ slightly from the t intervals of Table 2. ᵃThe fixed-hour comparison adds local start-hour indicators (reference 17:00) to the heat-avoided model; it was defined after the pre-specified results were available and fixed before fitting. Fixed-hour shares use the rise expected at an unchanged start hour and speed as their denominator. The recovered-weather sample (112,797 sessions, ≥850 runners) restores sessions whose local-day weather was completed at the edges of the download windows. The runner bootstrap (999 draws, seed 20261002, ≥820 runners resampled) refits the linked models in every replicate and reports 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Both use the main specification; each first reproduced its registered result under the pre-specified specification. Joint tests are cluster-robust Wald F statistics with runner-minus-one denominator degrees of freedom; participation uses its registered runner-by-year-month model.

title: Descriptive decomposition at P95 under alternative model specifications
note: All quantities compare a daily maximum of 30.51 °C (P95) with 15.40 °C (P50) under the fixed-hour benchmark and are estimates with 95% delta-method intervals; shares are fractions of the rise expected at an unchanged start hour and speed. ᵃThe model with start hour and weekday replaces the fixed-speed model with the version that adds local start-hour and weekday indicators. The runner-by-year-month model replaces the heat-avoided (with and without start-hour indicators), speed and whole-session heart-rate models with versions that include runner-by-year-month effects, keeping the main fixed-speed model.

title: From the expected rise with observed start times to the observed change in whole-session heart rate
note: Each level is the modelled change at P90 or P95 of the daily maximum relative to P50 under the main specification; each step is the difference between consecutive levels, so that the four steps sum to the difference between the rise expected with observed timing and the main whole-session estimate. Delta-method intervals use normal critical values, as in the decomposition, and the joint runner-clustered covariance of the six fits across the main sample, the fixed-speed cohort and the 18,626 common sessions (scores summed by runner). ᵃBootstrap intervals are 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles over 999 runner-resampled replicates in which every fit is refitted. The steps are descriptive and do not represent causal mediation. Table S4 gives the levels and the paired differences with t intervals, so the last digit of some P90 limits differs.

title: Daily probability of recording a run with heart rate before and after a hot day (Fig. 6a, model 3, percentage points)
note: Distributed-lag model of Table S12, column (3). Each row gives the change in the probability of recording a heart-rate run on the day that lies the stated number of days from a single day whose maximum is at P90 or P95 instead of P50, all other days held at P50; negative days are the days before the hot day (the leads of the model). ᵃThe cumulative column sums the rows from day 0 to the stated day, with intervals from the joint covariance. Because the daily maxima of consecutive days are strongly correlated, estimates for adjacent days trade off against each other, and the cumulative sums are more stable than the single days. Runner-clustered CR1 intervals with t critical values.

title: Timing of runs around hot days in distributed-lag and weekly models
note: The participation panel at the usual cell has ≥490,990 runner-days from ≥720 runners with the daily maximum on days t-7 to t+3, each entered with the three-knot spline of the main models; a run with heart rate was recorded on 17.8% of them. The cumulative contrast sums the same-day and lag contrasts, that is, the change in the number of runs over the eight days that follow a single hot day. Panel C uses ≥71,270 runner-weeks (local ISO weeks with seven panel days) from ≥720 runners, with counts of days below 0, 0 to 10, 20 to 25, 25 to 30 and at least 30 °C (reference 10 to 20 °C); minutes and kilometres sum the analysis sessions of each day, and workouts of any sport come from the workout metadata file of the FitRec release for the same runners. The weekly models have no weekday indicators. Seasonal pairs are dated at the week's Thursday. Runner-clustered CR1 intervals with t critical values. ᵃColumn (3) is the main specification, as for the session models.

title: Sensitivity of estimates for the timing of runs and participation in other activities under model 3
note: Checks added to the plan before estimation (Section B.6). Runner-by-year-month effects replace the runner effects and the seasonal pairs (in the weekly models, the month of the week's Thursday). ᵃTwo-way clustering is by runner and calendar date (daily models) or ISO week (weekly models), with t critical values on the smaller number of clusters minus one. For usual-cell runners, column (3) was fitted on the ≥230 runners with at least 80% of their sessions at the usual cell, where the exposure at the usual cell is least likely to be assigned at the wrong place. Any recorded run counts runs with or without heart rate. Outdoor cycling is split into transport (bike transport) and recreation (bike, mountain bike), under column (3) only, with the share of runner-days with each in parentheses.

title: Daily probability of recording a workout by sport and model (percentage points)
note: The participation panel has 503,410 runner-days from 729 runners, with the daily maximum at the usual cell. Outcomes come from the workout metadata file of the FitRec release for the same runners, whatever their heart-rate record, which has no location, dated in the runner's usual time zone; workouts with corrupt time stamps (outside 2000 to 2017) are excluded, a rule set during the analysis. Outdoor cycling combines bike, bike (transport) and mountain bike; walking and hiking combine walk, hiking and fitness walking; indoor training combines weight training, core stability, circuit training, elliptical, aerobics, yoga, pilates, gymnastics and stair climbing; all indoor sessions add treadmill running and indoor cycling. Runner-clustered CR1 intervals with t critical values. ᵃColumn (3) is the main specification.

title: Modification of the P90 versus P50 contrast by prior ambient heat in the main model
note: Each estimate describes the modification of the current-temperature contrast relative to the exposure-specific P50 for a 5 °C higher prior mean daily maximum, under the main specification (runner fixed effects, two annual sine–cosine pairs and day-of-week indicators, or the fixed-speed controls for heart rate at fixed speed). The models use the design matrices from the pre-specified analysis with the calendar-year indicators omitted. Parentheses show pointwise 95% confidence intervals from runner-clustered standard errors. ᵃThe weighted mean halves its weights every seven days; the 7-day equal-day mean is the registered window sensitivity. The supported increment was specified in advance as one within-runner standard deviation of the history variable (6.6 to 6.9 °C across histories and samples), computed from exposures only and rounded to the nearest 0.5 °C; because history enters linearly, those estimates are the estimates per 5 °C scaled by the increment over 5. Duration modifications are proportional changes in the duration ratio. Counts preceded by ≥ are lower bounds under the disclosure rule.

title: Modification of the P95 versus P50 contrast by prior ambient heat in the main model
note: Each estimate describes the modification of the current-temperature contrast relative to the exposure-specific P50 for a 5 °C higher prior mean daily maximum, under the main specification (runner fixed effects, two annual sine–cosine pairs and day-of-week indicators, or the fixed-speed controls for heart rate at fixed speed). The models use the design matrices from the pre-specified analysis with the calendar-year indicators omitted. Parentheses show pointwise 95% confidence intervals from runner-clustered standard errors. ᵃThe weighted mean halves its weights every seven days; the 7-day equal-day mean is the registered window sensitivity. The supported increment was specified in advance as one within-runner standard deviation of the history variable (6.6 to 6.9 °C across histories and samples), computed from exposures only and rounded to the nearest 0.5 °C; because history enters linearly, those estimates are the estimates per 5 °C scaled by the increment over 5. Duration modifications are proportional changes in the duration ratio. Counts preceded by ≥ are lower bounds under the disclosure rule.

title: Joint tests of interaction between prior ambient heat and current temperature in the main model
note: ᵃThe F test jointly assesses whether the two interaction coefficients between prior temperature and the current-temperature spline equal zero, with runner-clustered covariance and 2 numerator degrees of freedom. These global tests do not correspond to individual P90 or P95 contrasts, and the p values are nominal.

title: Prior ambient heat by exposure window, season and fitness
note: ᵃEach history term is the mean daily maximum at the runner's usual cell over the stated days before the session, centred at 20 °C and in 5 °C units, interacted with both current-temperature spline terms. The modification is the change in the P90 or P95 contrast relative to P50 per 5 °C of the term, and the level is the change in the outcome per 5 °C at a current 20 °C. Terms listed together come from one model. Fits use the design matrices from the weighted-history analysis under the main specification. The first row gives the estimate reported in Table S16. Runner-by-year-month effects replace the runner effects and the seasonal pairs. The fitness index is the mean heart rate of the runner's steady segments 28 to 42 days earlier, on sessions below the session-temperature P50, minus the speed-spline part of the fixed-speed model; 36% of the sessions have it, and its coefficient was 0.12 (0.06 to 0.18) beats·min⁻¹ per beat·min⁻¹. Intervals are runner-clustered CR1 with t critical values. Specified before estimation (Section B.4.2).

title: Heart rate at fixed speed by fitness and phase of the warm season (session-temperature P90 and P95 relative to P50)
note: Fixed-speed model of the main specification (runner fixed effects and seasonal pairs, with its speed spline, recorded minutes over 14 days and 28-day fitness speed, and no day-of-week indicators). ᵃPanel A adds the fitness index of Table S18 and compares the two fits on the same sessions with their joint covariance. Panel B interacts the session-temperature spline with the part of the warm season (Northern Hemisphere months; six months later in the Southern) in sessions of those months. Specified before estimation (Section B.4.2).

title: Heat exposure during prior runs and the heart-rate response to session temperature at fixed speed
note: This analysis addresses the secondary objective of prior recorded heat exposure. ᵃExposure is running time in recorded runs averaging at least 25 °C during the preceding 14 days, classified by each runner's own tertiles. The low category contains 87.7% of sessions, and 87.3% have no recorded prior hot running. Estimates are in beats·min⁻¹ at fixed speed from a runner fixed-effects model with a session-temperature spline interacted with exposure category, under the main specification (19,350 sessions, 669 runners); the model was first reproduced under the pre-specified specification. Changes are relative to 20 °C; a negative difference in the change would indicate attenuation. The minimum detectable difference at 28 °C with 80% power is about 1.6 beats·min⁻¹, three quarters of the whole rise.

title: Weekday and weekend responses at P95 (30.51 °C) relative to P50
note: Modelled change at P95 of the daily maximum (30.51 °C) relative to P50 (15.40 °C) within weekday and weekend sessions (Saturday and Sunday, local time), from the main specification with the day-of-week indicators replaced by a weekend indicator and its interaction with the daily-maximum spline. The difference is the weekend minus the weekday contrast; duration differences are proportional differences between the two duration ratios. Pointwise 95% intervals and p values use runner-clustered standard errors. The analysis plan named weekend status as the only effect modifier, to be reported on the additive scale with a formal interaction test. Joint Wald tests of the two interaction terms between the weekend indicator and the daily-maximum spline gave p < 0.001 for heat avoided, p = 0.952 for speed, p = 0.636 for duration and p = 0.001 for heart rate. The plan's weekend contrasts at 25 and 30 °C relative to 20 °C are in Table S3. ᵃHolm adjustment covers eight weekend contrasts across P90 and P95. The table shows the four contrasts at P95. Heart-rate models use 106,341 sessions from ≥810 runners with at least one admissible reading.

title: P95 versus P50 contrasts with and without adjustment for daily maxima on the following three days
note: The main specification has runner fixed effects, two annual sine–cosine pairs aligned by hemisphere and day-of-week indicators. Intervals are pointwise 95% runner-clustered CR1 intervals with t critical values. The fixed-speed models keep their speed spline, recorded minutes and 28-day fitness terms and have no day-of-week indicators. ᵃBoth fits use the same sessions, and the difference uses their joint runner-clustered covariance. The contrast against session temperature uses its own percentiles (P50 12.61 °C, P95 25.93 °C). Specified before estimation (Section B.5.2).

title: Daily maximum temperatures on the three days after a session, coefficients per 5 °C and joint tests
note: The main specification has runner fixed effects, two annual sine–cosine pairs aligned by hemisphere and day-of-week indicators. Intervals are pointwise 95% runner-clustered CR1 intervals with t critical values. Each model adds the daily maximum at the runner's usual cell on the three following local days, per 5 °C, to its own specification; the fixed-speed models keep their speed spline, recorded minutes and 28-day fitness terms and have no day-of-week indicators. 97.2% of main-sample sessions and 97.1% of the fixed-speed cohort have the three leads; 68.6% of main-sample sessions were recorded at the usual cell. Each cell gives the coefficient, its interval and its z value. ᵃThe joint test is a Wald F test of the three coefficients. For heart rate, future temperature cannot act on the session, so a non-zero lead indicates residual confounding by factors that vary over time⁹; for behaviour, a lead mixes confounding with anticipation of forecasts. Specified before estimation (Section B.5.2).

title: Lee-type bounds for selective recording at P95 relative to P50
note: The selection margin is the pre-specified participation outcome, recording a run with heart rate on the day, which changed at P95 by −0.61 percentage points (lower 95% limit −1.39) on a reference share of 17.7% of runner-days within 2 °C of P50. ᵃThe trimming share is that decline divided by the reference share. Partial residuals (the daily-maximum spline part plus the within-runner residual of the main specification) of sessions within 2 °C of P50 are trimmed from the top or the bottom by that share and compared with those within 2 °C of P95; under monotone selection the bounds contain the change among sessions that would be recorded on both kinds of day. Bootstrap limits are the 2.5th percentile of the lower and the 97.5th percentile of the upper bound over 199 runner-resampled replicates with the model held fixed. The spline contrast is the main estimate of Table 2.

title: Sensitivity of the main P95 (30.51 °C) versus P50 (15.40 °C) contrasts
note: Each row changes one aspect of the main specification (runner fixed effects, three-knot daily-maximum spline, two annual sine–cosine pairs and day-of-week indicators) and reports the P95 versus P50 contrast with pointwise 95% confidence intervals. ᵃSessions and runners refer to the behavioural outcomes; heart-rate models use the subset with at least one admissible reading. Runner-by-year-month effects absorb the seasonal terms, so that row is identical under the main and pre-specified specifications. Clustering by runner and date changes uncertainty only. All rows use the main-cohort daily-maximum percentiles as anchors; in the daily-mean row these anchors lie on the daily-mean scale, and the P95 contrast exceeds the daily-mean 99th percentile (29.3 °C) and involves extrapolation. The next two rows report duration in minutes and distance in kilometres. The row with equal runner weights gives each runner a total weight of one (weights 1/n, with n the runner's sessions), so that it describes the average runner rather than the average session; the final row evaluates the daily-mean model at the 50th and 95th percentiles of the daily mean itself. At P90 (27.64 °C), equal runner weights gave −2.54 (−2.74, −2.34), −0.062 (−0.100, −0.023), −0.3 (−5.0, 4.7) and −0.81 (−1.77, 0.14) for the four outcomes in column order, and the daily mean at its own P90 (22.81 °C) gave −1.57 (−1.77, −1.37), −0.033 (−0.058, −0.009), −2.3 (−5.3, 0.7) and −0.11 (−0.69, 0.47). Counts preceded by ≥ are lower bounds under the disclosure rule.

title: P90 and P95 contrasts relative to P50 with and without adjustment for precipitation, wind and solar radiation
note: The main specification has runner fixed effects, two annual sine–cosine pairs aligned by hemisphere and day-of-week indicators. Intervals are pointwise 95% runner-clustered CR1 intervals with t critical values. Precipitation is the total of the local day (mm), wind speed the mean of the hourly values of that day (m·s⁻¹) and solar radiation the sum over that day (MJ·m⁻²), from ERA5-Land at the cell of the session, entered as three linear terms. Panel A uses the ≥106,390 sessions with the three daily variables, from ≥820 runners (heart rate, ≥106,130 sessions from ≥810 runners). Each row compares the two fits on the same sample, so the estimates without the added terms can differ slightly from those of the full samples. ᵃThe difference between the two fits uses their joint runner-clustered covariance and was computed before rounding. Duration is shown as the percentage change, 100 × (exp(contrast) − 1), and its difference in log points × 100. Panel B uses the three variables at each runner's usual cell on each local day, in the ≥503,120 runner-days that have them, from ≥720 runners, and does not include every runner of the participation panel (Section B.5.3). Panel C uses the fixed-speed model (runner fixed effects and seasonal pairs, with its speed spline, recorded minutes over 14 days and 28-day fitness speed, and no day-of-week indicators) and adds the means of wind speed and of solar radiation (W·m⁻²) over the hours of the session, in ≥19,340 sessions from ≥660 runners. Section B.5.3 describes the variables, and Table S27 gives the coefficients of the added terms.

title: Coefficients for precipitation, wind speed and solar radiation
note: Coefficients of the terms added in Table S26, each with its pointwise 95% runner-clustered CR1 interval, from the models with the added terms. The terms are linear, so a coefficient is the change in the outcome per unit of the term, with temperature and the other added terms held fixed. For duration the coefficient is shown as the percentage change, 100 × (exp(coefficient) − 1), and for the probabilities it is in percentage points. ᵃIn panel C the model has no precipitation term (n/a), and the coefficient of solar radiation is per 100 W·m⁻² of mean radiation over the hours of the session.

title: Session composition on hot days at P90 (27.64 °C) and P95 (30.51 °C) relative to P50 (15.40 °C)
note: Each estimate is the modelled within-runner change at the 90th or 95th percentile of the daily maximum relative to its median, from the main specification of the behavioural outcomes (runner fixed effects, three-knot daily-maximum spline, two annual sine–cosine pairs and day-of-week indicators) or with runner-by-year-month effects, which absorb the seasonal terms and are unchanged from the pre-specified analysis. Walking share is the share of recorded time in which the speed between consecutive points was below the threshold; pause share is the share of the session span in recording gaps classified as pauses (Section A.2). This analysis was defined after the pre-specified results were available, and its specification was fixed before any outcome was computed. ᵃCounts preceded by ≥ are lower bounds under the disclosure rule.

title: Temperature distributions and within-runner support for the exposure contrasts
note: Daily-maximum comparisons in the main, sensitivity and participation analyses use the P50, P90 and P95 of the 106,600-session main cohort (15.40, 27.64 and 30.51°C). The fixed-speed heart-rate analysis uses session-temperature percentiles from its 19,350-session cohort. We calculate percentiles by linear interpolation with equal session weights. The complete-history cohort in Section B.4.1 has its own exposure percentiles. Main curves span P1 to P99 (−4.6 to 34.6°C), with spline knots at P10, P50 and P90 (4.1, 15.4 and 27.6°C) and basis centring at 20°C. ᵃSupport requires at least 10 runners within ±2°C of the reference, the target and both; every comparison meets this rule. Support counts are lower bounds rounded down to a multiple of 10. In panel B, all samples use daily maximum temperature except fixed-speed heart rate, which uses session temperature.
